To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Complex maternal antiretrovirals for prevention of mother to child transmission resulted in a substantial emergence of minor drug resistant HIV-1 variants.
the complex prophylaxis for prevention of vertical transmission of HIV- 1 resulted in a high emergence of drug-resistant HIV- 1 variants.
Complex prophylaxis for prevention of mother to child transmission of HIV- 1 results in a high frequency of AZT-resistant HIV -1 variants and a moderate frequency of NVP- resistant HIV- 1 variants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the emergence of drug-resistant HIV-variants in women receiving complex maternal antiretoviral prophylaxis for prevention of mother to child HIV-transmission.
the development of minor drug-resistant variants in HIV-positive women following complex prophlylaxis.
the development and evaluation of novel antiviral drugs and antiretrovirologic strategies in the context of HIV-1 infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study has shown that complex prophylaxis resulted to a lower level of resistance to NVP, but to a substantial level of resistance to AZT.
the complex prophylaxis regimen as recommended by WHO for prevention of vertical HIV-1 transmission in resource-limited setting is not the best option.
the complex regimen is not as good as the single dose regimen.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current WHO guidelines for prevention of mother to child transmission are insufficient to prevent emergence of drug-resistant virus and should be reconsidered.
the current WHO-guideline for prevention of mother to child HIV transmission in resource limited settings is effective in preventing vertical transmission but may select for resistance.

complex antiretrovival prophylaxis for the prevention of mother-to-infant HIV-transmission in resource-limited countries is associated with the selection of drug-resistant HIV-variants in a substantial proportion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
complex maternal antiretoviral regimens are associated with the development of minor HIV-1 variants resistant to antiretrovirals used in the regimen.

the WHO-recommended complex maternal antiretoviral prophylaxis is not optimal for prevention of HIV transmission from mother-to-child and that the current WHO-recommendation of starting AZT at gestational week 28 is suboptimal.
the complex prophylaxis regimen recommended by the WHO for resource-limited settings is associated with a substantial rate of emergence of minor drug-resistance variants.
